extracted.intended_audience: aspiring microfiction writers / participants in nycmidnight microfiction challenges
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for composing complete microfiction stories of three hundred words or less, covering structure, style, character, trimming, formatting, and reading/study practices. Geared toward writers learning to craft tight, standalone narratives with strong plot and economical language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of microfiction (length and standalone story)
rubrics_metrics.description: For our challenges, microfiction is defined as a story of three hundred words or less. Think one double-spaced page or less - although dialogue-heavy stories may extend past a single page. Shorter microfiction - fifty to one-hundred-word stories - are much shorter than a page and are closer to a paragraph long. Microfiction pieces stand on their own with a clear beginning, middle, and end. It’s not an excerpt of a longer piece, but its own complete story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a reader finishes a satisfying piece of microfiction, they’ll feel like they’ve glimpsed something finished, not needing any more context or backstory than what was given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize powerful plot and essential details
rubrics_metrics.description: Powerful plot makes a good story great - and in no medium is that distinction more important than microfiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use only the details that craft the narrative arc; leave enough ambiguity for readers to contemplate, but give concrete, critical information. The Hemingway six-word example shows how each clause must deliver new, critical information that advances the implied plot without wasting words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the cast few (fewer characters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Microfiction thrives when it’s kept simple. Be mindful that naming more than two characters can be difficult for the reader to follow. Keeping your character list as sparse as possible allows readers to get to know these characters more intimately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include only characters essential to the central arc of the story. Fewer characters means more depth for the main character; avoid similar or numerous names that strain reader memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show, don’t tell (use concrete, sensory detail)
rubrics_metrics.description: Broad concepts become meaningful when narrow details rope them into the concept. Get specific about what’s happening and show characters interacting with the world. Incorporate multiple senses to ground readers and anchor characters in time and space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than stating an emotion (e.g., 'El was lonelier than anyone in the world'), show actions or habits that convey it (standing at the edge of a party, awkward conversation). Ask how each emotion influences the character’s interactions in the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer strong nouns and verbs over adjectives and adverbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Opt for nouns and verbs that do the heavy lifting adjectives and adverbs are trying to do. Replace adverb+verb combinations with stronger verbs to save words and sharpen prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'sprinted' instead of 'ran swiftly'; 'slouched' vs 'sat lazily'. Limit adjectives (test one per sentence); choose the single strongest noun (e.g., 'tome' not 'big, heavy, old book'). Well-placed adjectives can spice prose, but use them sparingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your character (pre-draft character work)
rubrics_metrics.description: Start by knowing your character: who they are and how they interact with the world. Explore traits like how they handle conflict and deliver sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write notes on a card or scrap of paper to serve as a reference. Spending five or ten minutes on this can generate personality details that hook readers and keep character consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give characters distinctive voice and dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: If you use dialogue, make it unique to your character. Small subtleties in speech make lines feel authentic and distinguish characters from one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether a character speaks in run-on sentences, monosyllables, etc. Use these habits to make voice ring true and to set up conflict when voices clash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify motive and integrate movement (motive & movement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify what the character wants — motive gives the story clear stakes and moves the action forward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate motive with concrete action at key places. Characters acting on desires provide both plot propulsion and character definition, especially important in limited word counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine thought and action (don’t rely on only one)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many beginning writers choose thought or action exclusively; marrying the two propels the story while building character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples: all thought (no action) vs all action (no thought) vs action+thought. Combine internal perspective with concrete action in key moments so motive and emotion are clear without exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Less is more — every sentence must serve the arc (trimming philosophy)
rubrics_metrics.description: With fiction this short, trimming is everything. After drafting, ask of every sentence: does this serve the arc?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a detail is not fundamental, cut it. Remove backstory or side plots that don't contribute to the single strong story or image you’re crafting. Test by removing a detail and rereading to see if cohesiveness remains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pare descriptions and condense details (trimming words & making space)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pare down descriptions to the most powerful ones so remaining lines carry more weight and free up word count.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Condense scene-setting to one or two vivid details rather than many. Example shows reducing a 57-word description to a much shorter version that still captures setting while saving words for plot/action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer active voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Active voice generally uses fewer words and strengthens narrative voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'It can shield us from the sun' → 'it shields us from the sun.' Trimming a few words matters especially with 100–300 word limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trim perception verbs (avoid filtering via 'saw', 'felt', etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Perception verbs (think, feel, hear, see) can put a filter between reader and scene and add unnecessary words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eliminate or rework perception verbs so readers experience the object directly. Example: 'Lena saw the calendar...' → 'The calendar sat on the desk. Lena opened it to a circled date...' This frees words and increases urgency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting: use spacing and paragraph breaks to create illusion of space
rubrics_metrics.description: Creative formatting gives the illusion of space without adding words. Break into paragraphs (within reason) to avoid a rushed feel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally avoid spacing beyond double-spaced. Always start a new paragraph for a different character speaking to maintain clarity. Thoughtful pauses and line breaks let readers 'marinate' in the world longer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study exemplary microfiction (reading recommendations and analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Read solid examples of the form and analyze them with intention to learn what works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take notes and answer questions after each piece: What compelled you? Why? What didn't compel you? How many scenes/settings/characters? How do they structure sentences/voice? How do characters surprise you? What’s one thing you could incorporate into your style? Use award-winning pieces as study material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance ambiguity with concrete detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Leave room for compelling ambiguity so readers can contemplate unanswered questions, while still providing enough concrete details to invest them in the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hemingway example: each clause provides critical detail but leaves cause and actors partly unknown. Aim for a similar economy: give pivotal facts, omit unnecessary backstory, maintain narrative tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use community feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Connecting with other writers and getting feedback helps growth and refinement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post in forums, bounce ideas and resources off other writers, and seek reflections on crafting microfiction. Community critique can highlight which details are essential or dispensable.
